title: The strongest models capture eighty percent of the market, but moats last only three to six months
dek: As long as the market expands, cutting-edge models capture eighty percent of spending; but models become obsolete in three to six months, after which there's nearly no long tail, and moats evaporate instantly.
why: To understand the real risks in AI infrastructure and model businesses, rather than settling for hollow platitudes about ‘moats’ and ‘network effects’.
who: Investors and founders focused on AI infrastructure, model valuations, and strategic M&A who want to know whether moats are worth worrying about.
skip: The opening categorization of four investment mentalities is abstract and general; skip directly to the moat and network effects section.

points.h: Four investment mentalities; most investors haven't figured out which they use
points.body: Casado divides investors into four types: financial investors who only care about market size and SaaS metrics; productive investors who believe the underlying asset creates value, which forces out markets and business models; frontier investors in the 1960s-70s mode—pure YOLO betting that founders see what others don't, with no due diligence; speculation investors who ignore the underlying asset and only want to time market moves. His point isn't which is right, but that most investors don't know which logic they're actually using—they justify an investment with productive-investor reasoning but then judge the company by financial-investor standards of ‘revenue quality’, contradicting themselves.

points.h: Moat discussions mistake mechanism for shape; linearity is what actually matters
points.body: Casado notes ‘network effects’ appears in seventy percent of funding pitches but nobody agrees on the definition—some treat it as tautology (‘more users make the product better’), others mean the super-linear growth of telephone networks. The real question isn't what you call the moat, but whether it scales super-linearly, linearly, or sub-linearly as the company grows: only super-linear scaling is truly defensible; sub-linear scaling means challengers will catch up eventually, regardless of whether you call it ‘network effects’.

points.h: In expanding markets, moat anxiety is mostly irrelevant until growth stalls
points.body: From Casado's experience, companies don't want direct competition as long as the market is growing—there's too much white space to grab. Moats only truly determine winners once the market slows or shrinks. He notes that three years ago almost everyone said models and NeoCloud ‘have no moat’ and ‘poor revenue quality’, but if the market is large and still growing, these worries actually don't matter.

points.h: Models have three to six months before obsolescence; nobody switches to cheaper alternatives
points.body: Casado's conclusion: a leading-edge model's lifecycle is just three to six months—once it falls behind, there's almost no software-industry-style ‘long tail’, and you might lose the entire market instantly. But he corrects a common misunderstanding: enterprises automating all tasks they can and plateauing token use doesn't mean they'll switch to cheaper older models to save money. In the competitive equilibrium where startups fight each other, everyone will pay ten times more for the smartest model, because losing the intelligence race costs more than spending more money.

points.h: AI's biggest disruption: engineering productivity finally responds to capital
points.body: Casado revisits the mythical man month—the near-natural law in software engineering history that adding people slows projects down, and engineering efficiency never scales linearly with spending. Ten years ago, if five founders asked for a billion dollars, that money would either sit idle or explode the team. Now give twenty people a billion dollars and they can actually spend it and produce results—whether they earn back five billion or twenty, nobody knows. In his view, this is the industrial-revolution-level transformation AI brings.

points.h: NeoCloud and NeoLab are different things; power and chips are the real bottleneck
points.body: Casado distinguishes two often-conflated company types: NeoCloud provides GPUs, data centers, and other physical infrastructure whose end product is tokens; NeoLab is research spending on new model architectures, betting that ‘solving intelligence creates a business model automatically’—OpenAI and Anthropic started this way. He judges the industry's true bottleneck as neither capital nor debt but electrical power and chip supply, so most compute will concentrate in a few scaled giants, leaving a long tail for players with access to special resources.

points.h: He was attacked for arguing private markets are efficient, unlike his peers
points.body: Casado admits he's nearly alone in this view: he believes private markets are smart enough that prices already reflect risk, so he never tries to find ‘undervalued non-consensus targets’. Due diligence, he says, lowers risk rather than finding bargains. He's also been mobbed on Twitter for saying ‘betting non-consensus is dangerous’ and disagreed with Roloff's ‘venture capital is not an asset class, only twenty companies matter’—he thinks more capital into private markets creates more value instead of diluting the existing pool.

points.h: Strategic M&A fails when deals leak; discretion is the entire negotiation
points.body: Looking back at the Cursor, World Labs, and OpenRouter acquisitions, Casado distills a pattern: the buyer is really buying an option on a massive market, and the seller's job is proving to the buyer that the ‘inductive step’ works—you have a base business, then show you can plug into the buyer's platform and scale. Only founders or true strategists can have this conversation. His other lesson: boards often pressure founders to play competitors off each other or leak to media to raise the price, but it only shakes the deal. World Labs never leaked anything and closed smoothly; OpenRouter kept leaking to media and the process was painful.
